title: Thinking Like a Philosopher
objective: After this level you can take a new big question through the tree's toolkit: clarify the terms, test it with a thought experiment, and weigh the rival views.
summary: “Would it be good to live forever?” through the toolkit: clarify it, test it with Williams’s Makropulos case, and weigh his tedium argument against the replies.

cards.headline: Would it be good to live forever?
cards.body: Here’s a big question this tree hasn’t answered. Rather than hand you a verdict, this level takes it through the toolkit: clarify it, test it, weigh the rivals.

cards.headline: Step 1: pin down the question
cards.body: “Forever” could mean endless old age, which is not the interesting question. So philosophers sharpen it: suppose you stayed healthy and mentally sharp, indefinitely. Bernard Williams added two conditions for wanting such a life: it should clearly be you who lives forever, and that life should connect to the aims you have now.

cards.headline: Step 2: build a case
cards.body: In “The Makropulos Case” (1973), Williams borrowed a character from a play by Karel Čapek. Elina Makropulos took an elixir of life; at 342, she has reached a state of boredom and indifference. Williams argued that, given enough time, the deep desires that make us want a future would run out, and boredom would set in.

cards.headline: Step 3: weigh the rivals
cards.body: Nagel, Jonathan Glover and John Martin Fischer replied that an endless life needn’t grow dull: your interests could keep changing. Williams answered that swapping in new desires and a new character makes it unclear the later person is still you, breaking his first condition. The question remains controversial, and now you know how to join it.

cards.headline: Thinking Like a Philosopher: the big picture
learned: Step 1: pin down what the question means
Step 2: test it with a built case
Would living forever be good? Still debated

questions.prompt: In Bernard Williams’s thought experiment, Elina Makropulos has reached _____ at 342.

options.label: great wisdom and calm
options.rationale: That isn’t how Williams describes her.

options.label: memory loss
options.rationale: Her problem is boredom, not forgetting.

questions.explanation: At 342, her endless life has reached a state of boredom and indifference.

questions.prompt: Fischer says an immortal could avoid boredom by changing interests over time. What is Williams’s reply?

options.label: Changing interests would make an endless life shorter
With new desires and character, it’s unclear the later person is still you
Boredom is actually good for us in small doses
options.rationale: He treats boredom as the problem.

questions.explanation: Williams’s first condition is that it should clearly be you who lives forever; swapping in a new character threatens that.
